```{r, include = FALSE}
if (requireNamespace("pkgload", quietly = TRUE)) {
  pkgload::load_all(export_all = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
}
options(mcp_quiet = TRUE)
set.seed(42)
```

There are three main ways of doing model comparison in `mcp`:

 1. Compare any N `mcp` models using Leave-One-Out cross-validation (LOO-CV). Check out `loo(fit)`, `loo::loo_compare(loo1, loo2, ...)`, and `loo::loo_model_weights(loo1, loo2, ...)`.
 2. Flexible directional tests using `hypothesis(fit, "cp_1 > 40")` or `hypothesis(fit, "cp_1 > 40 & x_2 > x_1")`.
 3. Point-null Bayes factor tests using the Savage-Dickey density ratio, e.g., `hypothesis(fit, "cp_1 = 50")` or `hypothesis(fit, "x_2 = x_1")`.


```{r}
library(mcp)
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3)
```


# Some models to play with
We know quite a bit about human short-term memory. Namely, the average human has almost perfect recall when presented with 1-4 items (we remember them all), and then errors begin intruding when presented with more items [(Cowan, 2001)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11515286). We also know that memory is not infinite, so as $N \rightarrow \infty$, it has to plateau.

In other words, on "easy" trials with $N <= capacity$ items to be recalled, we expect a constant high binomial rate. When $N > capacity$, the rate declines. We specify a prior reflecting our a priori knowledge.

```{r}
model = list(
  recalled | trials(items) ~ 1,
  ~ 0 + items
)
prior = list(
  Intercept_1 = "dnorm(2, 1)", # high recall for easy trials
  cp_1 = "dnorm(4, 1)", # performance discontinuity around 4
  items_2 = "dnorm(-0.4, 1) T( , -0.2)" # performance deteriorates considerably
)

# A very simple model
model_simple = list(recalled | trials(items) ~ 1 + items)
```

Notice that `items` is used both as `trials` and x-axis. No problem.


Simulate some data using `fit$simulate()`:

```{r}
# Simulate data
df = data.frame(items = rep(1:9, each = 40), recalled = 1)

# Get just the model - no fit
empty = mcp(model, data = df, family = binomial(), sample = FALSE)

df$recalled = empty$simulate(
  empty, df,
  cp_1 = 4,
  Intercept_1 = 2.5,
  items_2 = -0.4
)

head(df)
```


Now fit it with and without the informative prior. We set `iter` fairly high because this model is not sampled efficiently. We will also add `sample = "both"` to sample *both* prior and posterior. We will need both to compute Bayes factors using `hypothesis()` later.

```{r, results = FALSE}
fit_default = mcp(model, data = df, family = binomial(), sample = "both", iter = 6000)
fit_info = mcp(model, data = df, prior = prior, family = binomial(), sample = "both", iter = 6000)
fit_simple = mcp(model_simple, data = df, family = binomial(), sample = "both", iter = 6000)
```

We plot them and add a few `ggplot2` layers. We jitter the raw data in the middle plot, just to give a sense of the densities.

```{r}
library(patchwork)
library(ggplot2)

plot(fit_default) +
  ggtitle("Default") +

  plot(fit_info) +
  ggtitle("Informed") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, color = "red", size = 0.2) +

  plot(fit_simple) +
  ggtitle("Simple")
```


# Bayes Factors using Savage-Dickey density ratios
You can compute Bayes Factors for point-null hypotheses using `hypothesis()`. For example, let's compare a model in which the change point in recall is fixed at four items with the fitted continuous model:

```{r, collapse=TRUE, R.options = list(width = 9999)}
equality = hypothesis(fit_default, "cp_1 = 4")
equality
```

Notice that `mcp` issues a warning when computing Savage-Dickey Bayes factors on default priors. The Savage-Dickey ratio divides by the prior density at the tested value, so the Bayes factor is only as meaningful as that prior. The wider the prior, the lower that density, and the more the Bayes factor favors the point null. If you obtained these results with a bespoke, substantive prior, you would interpret them as:

 * `hypothesis`: For internal convenience, `hypothesis` always re-arranges to test against zero. 
 * `mean`: The posterior mean of `cp_1 - 4`, i.e., of the left-hand side after re-arranging.
 * `lower` and `upper`: The interval width defaults to a 95% central posterior interval, but you can change it using `hypothesis(..., width = 0.8)`.
 * `BF`: The Savage-Dickey density ratio in favor of the point-null model. It is the posterior density divided by the prior density at the tested equality (here $\theta = \text{cp}_1$ and $\theta_0 = 4$):
 
   $$BF_{01} = \frac{p(\theta = \theta_0 \mid \text{data})}{p(\theta = \theta_0)}$$

   where $\theta$ is the tested parameter (or contrast), $\theta_0$ is the hypothesized point value, $p(\theta = \theta_0 \mid \text{data})$ is the posterior density, and $p(\theta = \theta_0)$ is the prior density. A $BF > 1$ favors the point-null model, $BF = 1$ favors neither model, and $BF < 1$ favors the continuous alternative.
 * `prob`: This is `NA` because equality is not an event with positive probability in the continuous model.

Equality tests are limited to named parameters and affine contrasts such as `Intercept_1 - Intercept_2 = 0`. Ratios, parameter products, exponentials, and other nonlinear expressions are rejected.

To convert a Bayes Factor to a posterior probability for the point-null model, supply your own prior probability for that model. For example:

```{r}
prior_null_prob = 0.25
posterior_model_prob = equality$BF * prior_null_prob /
  (equality$BF * prior_null_prob + 1 - prior_null_prob)
posterior_model_prob
```

Because point Bayes factors depend directly on the prior density, they require bespoke, substantively justified priors. For example, testing `cp_1 = 4` on `fit_info` runs without warnings because an explicit prior was provided, yielding a substantially different Bayes factor:
 
```{r, R.options = list(width = 9999)}
hypothesis(fit_info, "cp_1 = 4")
```

The [default prior on change points](../articles/default_priors.html#change-points) is flat across the observed range of $x$, so it rarely represents an actual prior belief about the change point. Use an informed prior for point-null hypothesis tests.



# Directional and combinatoric tests
Maybe we just want to test a few directional hypotheses. For example:

 * Does recall begin to deteriorate when `cp_1 > 3`?
 * Is the change point in the interval `cp_1 > 3.5 & cp_1 < 4.5`?
 * The only constraint is your imagination. How about all hypotheses we may have at once? `cp_1 > 3.5 & cp_1 < 4.5 & items_2 < -0.4 & Intercept_1 > 2.5`, and a contrasting hypothesis `(cp_1 < 3.5 | cp_1 > 4.5) & items_2 > -0.4 & Intercept_1 < 2.5`. Each hypothesis is tested against its complement, i.e., all draws where it is false.

```{r, R.options = list(width = 9999)}
hypothesis(fit_info, c(
  "cp_1 > 3",
  "cp_1 > 3.5 & cp_1 < 4.5",
  "cp_1 > 3.5 & cp_1 < 4.5 & items_2 < -0.4 & Intercept_1 > 2.5",
  "(cp_1 < 3.5 | cp_1 > 4.5) & items_2 > -0.4 & Intercept_1 < 2.5"
))
```

Comparing the Bayes factors shows which hypothesis received the larger update from prior to posterior.

There are more examples [in the documentation for `hypothesis`](../reference/hypothesis.html), including how to test group-level deviations and [relative changes between segments](../articles/formulas.html#relative-changes-between-segments).

`mcp` evaluates the directional hypothesis for both posterior and prior draws. The returned `prob` is the posterior probability by default, or the prior probability with `prior = TRUE`; the Bayes factor is the posterior odds divided by the prior odds:

$$BF_{10} = \frac{P(H \mid \text{data}) \,/\, [1 - P(H \mid \text{data})]}{P(H) \,/\, [1 - P(H)]}$$

where $H$ is the stated directional hypothesis, $P(H \mid \text{data})$ is its posterior probability, and $P(H)$ is its prior probability.

```{r, R.options = list(width = 9999)}
hypothesis(fit_info, "cp_1 > 3.5 & cp_1 < 4.5")

# ... is identical to
prob = function(fit, prior = FALSE) {
  draws = as_draws_df(fit, prior = prior)
  mean(draws$cp_1 > 3.5 & draws$cp_1 < 4.5)
}

post_prob = prob(fit_info, prior = FALSE)
prior_prob = prob(fit_info, prior = TRUE)
BF = (post_prob / (1 - post_prob)) / (prior_prob / (1 - prior_prob))

print(c(post_prob = post_prob, BF = BF))
```



# Cross Validation
We can use the cross-validation from the `loo` package to compare the predictive performance of `mcp` models. Use `loo()` to compute the expected log pointwise predictive density (ELPD) or `waic()` for the Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC) for each model, and then compare them using `loo::loo_compare()`.

The strength of LOO-CV is that you can compare any N models, as long as they are models of the same data. In general, LOO-CV is the only inferential method for non-nested models in `mcp`. For example:

 * The existence of one or several change points. The [article on Poisson change points](../articles/poisson.html) contains an example of comparing a change-point model to a model without change points.
 * Models that differ by several parameters.
 * Comparing different priors.


## What is LOO-CV?
You can read more about Leave-One-Out Cross Validation elsewhere, but briefly, it does this:

 1. Computes the posteriors using all data *less one data point* (hence "leave one out"). 
 2. Computes the posterior predictive density at the left-out data point (out-of-sample data). For example, if the posterior predictive distribution is normal, a data point near its mean has higher density (it is less "surprising") than if it is at $z = -3$. Better predictions mean higher densities, i.e., less surprisal.
 3. Repeats steps 1-2 for all observed data and multiplies these densities to get the combined predictive density at unobserved data. Multiplying is the same as summing in log-space, and the latter has the advantage of being computationally much more feasible. Hence the name "expected log pointwise predictive density" (ELPD). The higher the ELPD, the better.

Refitting the model once per data point would be slow. `loo()` approximates it from a single fit using Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO). The Pareto $k$ diagnostics flag data points where this approximation is unreliable.

As with Bayes factors, LOO-CV can prefer simpler models. A parameter that mostly fits noise in the observed data makes predictions for left-out data worse. If it does too little to improve those predictions, it is a net negative for predictive accuracy, and the simpler model will be preferred.

Also, if the data is reasonably informative (it almost always is), LOO-CV is much less influenced by priors than Bayes factors. For LOO, the priors can more be thought of as regularization (shrinking estimates towards plausible values) than as the point of departure which all our inferences are relative to (Bayes Factors).


## Applied example
We can look at the loo for one model:
```{r}
loo_info = loo(fit_info)
loo_info
```

This is not terribly informative in and of itself. $looic = -2 * elpd_{loo}$ as are the corresponding SEs, so that is just a matter of scale. What ELPD tells you is that the product of the densities of all left-out data points is approximately $exp(`r round(loo_info$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"])`) \sim 10 ^ {`r round(loo_info$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"] / log(10))`}$, a vanishingly small number because we multiply many small numbers. This is mentally hard to interpret because the density at a given point is only meaningful relative to the full distribution. Furthermore, it depends on the size of the dataset (the more small densities you multiply, the smaller the ELPD).

What is interesting is the *relative* differences in these predicted densities. We can compare the models using `loo::loo_compare()`. Save the results as separate objects if you want to reuse them or save them for later.

```{r, collapse=TRUE}
loo_default = loo(fit_default)
loo_simple = loo(fit_simple)

loo::loo_compare(loo_default, loo_info, loo_simple)
```

The top row is the preferred model, here the second model passed to `loo_compare()` ("model2", i.e., `fit_info`). Read each `elpd_diff` relative to its `se_diff`: `fit_default` is practically indistinguishable from `fit_info`, and the simple model is only somewhat worse. So the informed prior adds little predictive accuracy, and the evidence for a change point over a straight line is modest.

In recent versions of `loo`, `loo_compare()` reports `p_worse` (the estimated probability that a model is worse than the best model) alongside diagnostic flags (`diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`) based on [Sivula et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1214/25-BA1569).

These diagnostics highlight when the normal approximation underlying `se_diff` and `p_worse` is unreliable. For example, `|elpd_diff| < 4` flags that models have very similar predictive performance and should be treated as practically indistinguishable (as between `model2` and `model1` here), while `N < 100` warns of small-sample uncertainty underestimation. See the [LOO glossary](https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html) or `?loo::loo-glossary` for details on all diagnostic flags.

You could do the same using `waic()`. WAIC is asymptotically equivalent to LOO-CV but less robust to influential data points, so `loo()` is generally preferred. The results are often practically identical.

```{r, collapse=TRUE}
waic_default = waic(fit_default)
waic_info = waic(fit_info)
waic_simple = waic(fit_simple)

loo::loo_compare(waic_default, waic_info, waic_simple)
```

## Stacking
The `loo` package contains many other useful functions. For example, if prediction is your goal, it is often optimal to *combine* models rather than letting the "winner-takes-it-all" do all the predicting. This is also called *stacking*:

```{r}
loo::loo_model_weights(list(
  default = loo_default, 
  info = loo_info, 
  simple = loo_simple
))
```

This means that once `info` (`fit_info`) has done its "predicting", the others add very little over and above that. If you want to learn about how well they predict relative to each other, use `loo::pseudobma_weights()`, which weights each model proportional to $\exp(\text{ELPD})$.

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
future::plan(future::sequential)
```
